#en:
Didn't sleep again.

Hips still remember the crash couch, even when it is just a bunk welded to a half-rusted frame. Funny how the body clings to routine long after the orders stop. Lights out, gear stacked, weapon at arm's reach. No CO, no duty roster, but I still wake on the minute before the alarm I do not set.

Redacted Division. We picked the name as a joke, sitting in that gutted briefing room with the projectors still cycling through half-deleted slides. Now it sticks to us like gun oil. Files gone, pay records blank, commendations scrubbed. Like we were never there. Except my shoulder still aches where shrapnel went through during that corridor push and Elena Carrow still rolls her ankle before a fight because she swears it saved her life once. Ghosts do not limp. We do.

Dana Kostova said tonight that we are freer than we have ever been. Her words, clipped like she was still reporting to someone. Maybe she believes it. Maybe she needs to. I watch her eyes when she says it and all I see is someone measuring blast radii in her head. She has not stopped doing that since the operation where the map was wrong and the civilians were in the wrong tower. Wrong. That is generous. The map we got was curated. Someone made a decision. We executed it. Then we were told our helmet cam feeds were corrupted in transit.

Kira Haldane does not talk about that deployment. She just maintains the rifles like they are all that is left holding her together. You can tell which ones were hers in the old unit; she runs a finger along the barrel before she racks them. Another ritual trying to paper over the cracks. Renee Calder pretends not to remember, cracks jokes about how we were all too green to see the signs. Mira Salcedo does remember. I know because she will not stand within sightline of anyone wearing an old-issue patch from that theater. We were told the insurgent stronghold had to go. We were told the signatures were hostile. Later, in the dark corners of the debrief, I heard an officer say "acceptable trade." That phrase still tastes like copper.

We walked away after that, in different stages. Some filed resignation that never processed. Some just did not report in. I followed them when the first arrest warrant was issued for "data tampering" and we all recognized the face. He had been the only one stubborn enough to print out the raw sensor logs before the purge. Official line said he falsified them. His body never turned up. Our record did not just get sealed; it was being rewritten. If the story does not match the blood on your boots, you either change the story or burn the boots. Command chose the first. We chose the second.

Abandoning official command felt like cutting my own spine out. Years of drilled instinct do not vanish because you toss a uniform into a recycler. I still hear the cadence when I move. Formation spacing. Threat sectors. Even in this cramped hold where we squat between runs, my brain assigns fire arcs. I do not know how to be anything else. That is the worst part. It is not that they betrayed us. It is that they built us so well we still want to flinch to attention when some new voice barks an order.

Redacted Division pretends we are leaderless, just a circle of equals, but everyone still glances at Kira before we break atmosphere. Old roles die slower than reputations. We run contracts now that would have had us court-martialed once. Asset extractions. Burn jobs. Ship jacks. No insignia, no chain, just credits and a list of coordinates. We tell ourselves we pick our targets. We do not hit hospitals or schools or relief ships. We have lines, we say. But every month those lines look thinner.

Long stakeouts used to be the worst part of the job. Hours on some blasted ridge or baking rooftop, watching a doorway that never opened, pulse crawling from boredom to dread and back again. It was strange how boredom and fear braided together until you could not tell them apart. You sit there long enough, you start wanting something to happen, anything, just to prove you are not already dead and dreaming in your armor. That is where the danger lives. Right on that edge where survival and savagery start sharing a face. Every week out there shaved that edge a little sharper. Fewer questions asked when a shadow moved wrong. Fewer warnings shouted in a language you half-understood.

Those habits did not go away when we cut loose. If anything, the leash snapping only made the dog meaner. I have seen Elena put two rounds into a runner's back because he twitched toward a console. Maybe he was calling reinforcements. Maybe he was trying to surrender on a frequency she did not care about. I did not stop her. The line between staying alive and becoming the thing we used to hunt is not a line anymore; it is fog. Some days I think we are already on the wrong side and just too deep in to notice.

I catch myself justifying what we do now the same way I used to justify deployments. "We take from bastards who deserve it." "We hit facilities that have skeletons in their foundations." Dana digs up the contracts, shows us the dossiers with all the ugly little footnotes. Human trials off-grid. Smuggled weapons. Black budgets written in blood. It is easier to breach a lab when you have already decided everyone inside is guilty. But I know how files can be massaged. I saw it happen once from the other end.

What keeps me here? Part habit, part fear of what waits if I walk away. Civvy life is not made for people who can clear a room in six seconds and sleep through nothing but ordnance. There is also loyalty, though I do not say that out loud. Not to flags or mottos anymore, but to the handful of faces that were there when the building came down, who dragged me out of broken steel and did not ask if I still believed. I owe Kira my life twice over. Elena caught a round meant for me. Mira patched a hole in my side with a dressing and a lie to the medevac techs. I walk because they walk. If we are going to hell, at least I will recognize the silhouettes.

Sometimes I dream about that last official briefing we sat in. The screen flickered, the map glowed, and the major recited words someone else had written. Threat indices, collateral estimates, authorizations. I remember staring at the line that said "post-action media narrative: localized unrest." That was the first time I thought about who writes the story when the guns cool. Now, in this little metal box, I am trying to write my own, and it is not coming out clean.

Tomorrow we hit another target. Supposedly a private black site, the kind that learned all the wrong lessons from the programs we bled for. The intel says they are doing the same experiments under a different franchise banner, chopping up the same kind of lives under a new logo. Maybe if we break their machines, it makes what we did back then matter a little less. Maybe that is just another lie.

I used to sign logs with my full name, rank, unit. Now I scratch three letters on the inside of my gauntlet and tell myself it is enough: R D V.

The V stands for Velez. I am trying not to forget that part.
zh:
又没睡。

髋部仍记得碰撞座椅，即便那只是一张焊在半锈框架上的铺位。有趣的是，命令停下之后很久，身体仍紧抓惯例。熄灯、装备码好、武器在一臂之内。没有指挥官、没有值勤表，可我仍在没设的闹钟前一分钟醒来。

涂黑师。我们选这个名字是当玩笑，坐在那间被掏空的简报室里，投影仪还在循环半删的幻灯片。如今它像枪油一样黏着我们。档案没了，薪资记录空白，嘉奖被抹掉。像我们从没在那儿。只是我的肩膀仍在某次走廊推进中被弹片穿透的地方隐隐作痛，而埃琳娜·卡罗在战斗前仍会活动脚踝，因为她赌咒说那曾救过她一命。鬼不瘸。我们瘸。

达娜·科斯托娃今晚说我们比任何时候都自由。她的话，像仍在向某人汇报一样短促。也许她信。也许她需要信。她说这话时我看她的眼睛，我看到的只是有人在脑子里测量爆炸半径。自那次地图错了、平民在错塔里的行动以来，她一直没停下这么做。错了。那是客气。我们拿到的那张地图是被策展过的。有人做了决定。我们执行了。然后我们被告知我们的头盔摄像头素材在传输中损坏了。

基拉·霍尔丹不谈那次部署。她只是维护步枪，像那是唯一还把她拢在一起的东西。你能看出旧部队里哪些是她的；她把枪架上架前会用手指顺着枪管捋一下。又一个试图糊住裂缝的仪式。蕾妮·卡尔德假装不记得，开玩笑说我们当时都太嫩、看不见迹象。米拉·萨尔塞多记得。我知道，因为她不站在任何戴那战区旧发臂章之人的视线之内。我们被告知叛军据点必须铲除。我们被告知那些特征信号是敌对的。后来，在述职的黑暗角落里，我听到一个军官说"可接受交换"。那句话至今尝起来像铜。

那之后我们在不同的阶段走开了。有些人提交了从未被处理过的辞呈。有些人只是不再报到。第一份"数据篡改"逮捕令发出时我跟着他们，而我们全都认出了那张脸。他是唯一固执到在清洗前打印出原始传感器日志的人。官方说法说他伪造了它们。他的尸体从未出现。我们的记录不只是被封存；它在被改写。要是故事与你靴子上的血不符，你要么改故事，要么烧靴子。指挥部选了前者。我们选了后者。

抛弃正式指挥部感觉像把自己脊椎砍出来。多年的操练本能不会因为你把一套制服丢进回收机就消失。我移动时仍听见那个节拍。队形间距。威胁扇区。即便在这间我们跑活之间蜗居的逼仄货舱里，我的脑子仍在分配射击弧。我不知道怎么成为别的。那是最糟的部分。不是他们背叛了我们。是他们把我们造得太好，以至于某个新声音喊命令时我们仍想立正稍息。

涂黑师假装我们无领导，只是一个平等的圈子，可每个人在脱离大气前仍会瞟基拉一眼。旧角色比名声死得慢。我们如今跑那些当年会让我们上军事法庭的合同。资产提取。焚毁作业。劫船。没有徽记，没有链条，只有信用币和一列坐标。我们告诉自己我们挑目标。我们不碰医院、学校或救援船。我们有线，我们说。可每个月那些线看起来更细。

漫长的潜伏曾经是这份工作最糟的部分。在某道荒芜山脊或滚烫屋顶上耗上几个小时，盯着一扇从不打开的门，脉搏从无聊爬到恐惧再爬回来。奇怪的是无聊和恐惧如何缠在一起，直到你分不清。你在那儿坐得够久，就开始想要有什么事发生，任何事，只为证明你还没死、还在装甲里做梦。危险就住在那儿。就在生存和野蛮开始共用一张脸的边缘上。外面的每一周都把那道边磨得更锋利一点。当影子移动得不对时，问的问题更少。用你半懂的语言喊的警告更少。

那些习惯在我们脱离时没有消失。如果说有什么变化，绳子一断只让狗更凶。我见过埃琳娜往一个逃跑者的背上打两枪，只因他朝一个控制台抽搐了一下。也许他在呼叫增援。也许他想在他不在乎的频率上投降。我没有阻止她。活着和变成我们过去猎杀的东西之间的界线不再是一条线；是雾。有些日子我觉得我们已经在错的那一侧，只是陷得太深而没注意到。

我发觉自己在用从前为部署辩护的同样方式为我们现在做的事辩护。"我们从活该的混蛋那里拿东西。""我们打那些地基里有骷髅的设施。"达娜挖出合同，给我们看那些带着所有丑陋小脚注的档案。账外人体试验。走私武器。用血写的黑预算。当你已经决定里面每个人都有罪时，炸开一间实验室更容易。可我知道文件能怎么被揉捏。我曾从另一端见过一次。

是什么让我留在这儿？一部分是习惯，一部分是怕走开后等着什么。平民生活不适合作六秒清空一个房间、除了爆炸声什么也睡不沉的人。也有忠诚，尽管我不说出声。不再对旗帜或格言，而是对那几个在楼塌时在场、把我从断裂的钢里拖出来、没问我是否还相信的面孔。我欠基拉两条命。埃琳娜接住了一发冲我来的子弹。米拉用一块敷料和一个对医疗后送技工撒的谎补好了我侧面的一个洞。我走因为他们走。如果我们要去地狱，至少我会认得那些剪影。

有时我梦见我们坐过的那最后一次正式简报。屏幕闪烁，地图发亮，少校背诵别人写的话。威胁指数、附带损伤估计、授权。我记得盯着那行"行动后媒体叙事：局部骚乱"。那是我第一次想，枪声冷却后是谁写故事。如今，在这只小铁盒里，我试图写自己的，而它写出来不干净。

明天我们打另一个目标。据说是一处私人黑站，那种从我们为之流血的计划里学错了所有教训的。情报说他们在另一个连锁品牌的旗号下做同样的实验，在新的标志下剁碎同样类型的生命。也许要是我们砸了他们的机器，就能让当年我们做的事稍微没那么要紧。也许那只是又一个谎。

我以前用全名、军衔、部队签日志。如今我在护手内侧划三个字母，告诉自己那够了：R D V。

V 代表贝莱斯。我正努力不忘记那一部分。

#en:
I used to think the worst thing that could happen in a day was the guy upstairs dropping weights at oh-five-hundred or the damned faucet in the kitchenette never fully shutting off. That drip used to drive me crazy on rest days. Funny, how that was what I thought stress was. I would sit on my bunk, patching up an old field jacket or sewing a knee on my fatigues, not because supply was short, just because my hands needed to be busy. Habit. Routine. Take something frayed and make it look inspection-ready. Back then the biggest crisis was whether the sergeant would notice a crooked stitch.

Lately I catch myself walking the parts of town command used to warn us off. The alleys where the street clinics don't ask names, where the bars don't log tabs, where nobody flinches when they hear automatic fire out past the docks. First it was just to clear my head after shift, then it became the only place my head would actually clear. I knew which corners the black-bag recruiters used, which stairwells smelled like old chem smoke and coolant. I told myself I was doing "presence patrols" out of habit, but I never filed a report.

There was this one night outside a dive near the freight yards. Some kid in a cheap jacket bumped my shoulder, hand sneaking toward my pocket. Muscle memory kicked in: step, pivot, wrist-lock. I remember how fast he folded, how his eyes went wide when I pushed him to the wall without even trying. I did not draw a weapon, did not even raise my voice. Just leaned in, let him see I was not afraid of him, or anyone he knew. He apologized, stammering, swore he did not mean anything by it. I let him go, but the part that stuck with me was not the almost-mugging. It was the way my heart slowed down after, the way the street seemed to give me a wider berth. It was disturbingly easy to enjoy that.

Caleb used to say the uniform was just cloth, that what mattered was who we were underneath it. He did not see how deep the seams ran. Even off-duty I ironed my shirts, patched my cuffs, polished boots no one inspected. Old habits from campaigns where an unbuttoned collar meant you were too tired to live through the next breach. Now, in Rogue Unit, there is no dress code, but I still find myself darning holes in the same old trousers instead of buying new ones. Everyone jokes that I am the squad quartermaster without a storehouse. The truth is, I am afraid if I stop caring about the small things, I will lose whatever line is left between soldier and something worse.

We all carry ghosts from those last official deployments. Mara never talks about the evac we were ordered to stand down on, but I have heard her grinding her teeth in her sleep. Jared will drink himself halfway under a table before he mentions the intel feed we got scrubbed before the tribunal, the one that did not match the brief we were given. Caleb still believes, or pretends to, that somebody up the chain simply "made a mistake." I remember the after-action debriefs, the careful phrasing, the statistics used like bandages over bodies we never got to see. Somewhere between those memos and the graveside detail, trust started bleeding out.

Rogue Unit is what is left when faith in the machine snaps but the training does not. We still stack on doors like we did in uniform, still clear rooms by reflex. Orders just come from a smaller table now. No flags on the wall, just a battered ops board and printed photos with faces circled. I wish I could say we are better this way, more honest, but there is a kind of freedom in not having to pretend the objectives are clean. We pick our contracts, tell ourselves we are balancing scales nobody else will touch. Some days I believe that. Some days I hear the old commands echoing in my head and I am not sure whose voice is giving them anymore.

My partner back then loved the uniform more than the person inside it, I think. There was always another family issue, another crisis, another favor that needed pulling strings. Their needs filled every off-duty hour: moving boxes, fixing visas, smoothing over arguments, visiting relatives who only called when they wanted something. I kept saying it was temporary, that once this deployment ended or that promotion posted, I would get to have a say. Instead, my world shrank down to their schedule and the next set of orders. One day I caught myself introducing myself as "his girl" before I used my own name. That was when I realized somewhere along the line I had stopped being a person and become a role, another resource to be allocated.

Walking through those bad parts of town, I started to feel more like myself than I did at home. That should have been the warning. When the first rumors surfaced about that operation we are not supposed to mention, the one with the casualty numbers that never made it onto any official ledger, I heard them in a bar that smelled like grease and cheap liquor, from people who should not have known the grid coordinates. I went back to the barracks and listened to the official brief the next morning, watched the holo-map neatly omit whole districts. That was the day Mara stopped saluting the big screens, and Jared started keeping copies of raw telemetry "just in case."

We did not all leave at once. It was more like a slow leak. Caleb tried to route complaints through channels until the channels closed around his throat. I got written up twice for "tone" in debriefs, then quietly reassigned to clerical support as if my trigger finger had gone bad. Mara vanished for a month, officially on compassionate leave, and came back with eyes that did not match her smiles. The final straw was not some grand revelation. It was sitting in our tiny apartment, listening to that damned faucet drip, sewing up a rip in my partner's jacket while he complained about a delayed shipment, and realizing I was more furious about a dry cleaning bill than the bodies we were supposed to forget. My anger had nowhere honest to go.

Rogue Unit did not recruit me with promises of justice. They just handed me a file, a burner, and a chance to stop pretending I did not see what we had done. I am not naive enough to think we are the good ones now. We are people who knew how to break things efficiently, and someone found a way to point us at different targets. But here, at least, my name is my own again. I fix my own gear, mend my own clothes, decide which lies I am willing to live with. And when I walk through those dangerous streets now, heads turn for what I chose to become, not the insignia stitched to my chest.

Still, some nights I hear that faucet. Some nights the drip sounds like a metronome counting down to the day we get caught or killed, and I wonder if we ever really left the old command behind or if we are just another off-the-books unit in a longer chain of deniability. I try not to think about the ops we took without asking who really signed the payments, about the way certain zones always seem to be redacted on our own maps. You can only ignore the patterns for so long before you have to decide whether you are going to follow them to the end or tear them apart with your bare hands.
zh:
我以前以为一天里能发生的最糟的事，是楼上那家伙在五点砸杠铃，或小厨房里那只该死的水龙头从不完全关严。那滴答在休息日曾把我逼疯。好笑，我当时以为那就是压力。我会坐在铺位上，补一件旧野战夹克或给制服缝一块膝盖，不是因为补给短缺，只是因为我的手需要忙起来。习惯。日常。拿一件磨损的东西，让它看起来像能通过检查。那时最大的危机是军士会不会注意到一道歪针脚。

近来我发觉自己走在指挥部曾警告我们避开的那些城区。那些街头诊所不问名字的巷子、酒吧不记欠账的地方、没人听见码头那边传来自动射击就畏缩的地方。起初只是班次后清空脑袋，然后它成了唯一真能让我脑袋清空的地方。我知道黑袋招募者用哪些角落、哪些楼梯间闻起来像旧药剂烟和冷却液。我告诉自己我在出于习惯做"存在巡逻"，可我从不提交报告。

有那么一晚，在货运场附近一间廉价酒吧外。一个穿廉价夹克的小子撞了我肩膀，手往我口袋摸。肌肉记忆启动了：侧步、转身、锁腕。我记得他多快就软了，我甚至没使劲把他推到墙上时他眼睛睁得多大。我没拔武器，甚至没提高声音。只是凑近，让他看到我不怕他，也不怕他认识的任何人。他道歉，结结巴巴，赌咒说他不是那个意思。我放他走了，可留在心里的不是那场几乎被抢。是之后我的心如何慢下来、街道似乎如何给我让出更宽的空间。令人不安地容易享受那个。

卡莱布以前说制服只是布，要紧的是我们底下是什么。他没看见那些接缝有多深。即便休班我也熨衬衫、补袖口、擦没人检查的靴子。那是从前战役的老习惯——那时一颗没扣好的领子意味着你累得活不过下次破门。如今，在亡命部队里没有着装规定，可我仍发觉自己在补同一条旧裤子上的洞，而不是买新的。大家都开玩笑说我是没有仓库的小队军需官。事实是，我怕要是我停止在乎小事，我就会失去士兵和更糟的东西之间剩下的那条线。

我们都带着那些最后正式部署的鬼。玛拉从不谈我们被命令按兵不动的那次撤离，可我听过她睡梦中磨牙。贾里德会把自己喝到桌子底下才提起那份在法庭前被清洗的情报流，那份和我们收到的简报不符的。卡莱布仍相信，或假装相信，指挥链上某人只是"犯了个错"。我记得那些行动后述职、那些小心的措辞、那些像绷带一样盖在我们从未见到的尸体上的统计数字。在那些备忘和墓地勤务之间的某处，信任开始流血。

亡命部队是对机器的信仰断裂、但训练没有时剩下的东西。我们仍像穿制服时一样在门口堆叠、仍凭反射清房间。命令只是现在来自更小的一张桌子。墙上没有旗帜，只有一块破旧的行动板和打印的、圈了面孔的照片。我希望我能说我们这样更好、更诚实，但不必假装目标干净里有一种自由。我们挑合同，告诉自己我们在平衡没别人会碰的天平。有些日子我信。有些日子我听见旧命令在脑子里回响，我不确定是谁的声音在发它们。

我那时的搭档，我想，爱制服胜过爱里面的人。总又有个家庭问题、又一场危机、又一份需要走动关系的人情。他们的需求填满每一个休班的小时：搬箱子、办签证、抹平争吵、探访那些只在想要什么时才打电话的亲戚。我一直说那是临时的，等这次部署结束或那次晋升下来，我就能有发言权。结果我的世界缩到他们的日程和下一批命令。有一天我逮到自己在用自己名字之前先把自己介绍成"他的姑娘"。就是那时我意识到一路上某处我已不再是一个人、而成了一个角色、一份待分配的资源。

走在城里那些糟糕的地方，我开始感觉比在家更像我。那本该是警告。当关于那次我们不许提的行动、那个从未进入任何官方账簿的伤亡数字的第一批传言浮出时，我在一间闻起来像油脂和廉价烈酒的酒吧里听到它们，从一个本不该知道网格坐标的人嘴里。我回到营房，听了第二天早晨的官方简报，看着全息地图干净地略过整个城区。那天玛拉停止了对大屏幕敬礼，贾里德开始留存原始遥测的副本"以防万一"。

我们不是一起走的。它更像一次缓慢的渗漏。卡莱布试着把投诉走渠道，直到渠道在他喉咙周围合拢。我因为在述职里的"语气"被记了两次警告，然后被悄悄调到文书支援，像我的扣扳机手指坏了。玛拉消失了一个月，官方说是事假，回来时眼睛和她的微笑对不上。最后一根稻草不是什么宏大的启示。是坐在我们的小公寓里，听着那只该死的水龙头滴答，缝着搭档夹克上的一道裂口，而他抱怨一批延误的货运，然后意识到我对一张干洗账单比对那些我们该忘记的尸体更愤怒。我的怒火无处可去。

亡命部队招我不是用正义的承诺。他们只是递给我一份档案、一部一次性通讯器，以及一个停止假装我没看见我们做过什么的机会。我还没天真到以为我们现在是好人。我们是懂得如何高效破坏东西的人，而有人找到了办法把我们指向不同的目标。可在这儿，至少我的名字又是我自己的。我修自己的装备、补自己的衣服、决定哪些谎言我愿意与之共处。而如今当我走过那些危险的街道时，人们转头是因为我选择成为的样子，而不是缝在我胸口的徽记。

不过，有些夜里我听见那只水龙头。有些夜里那滴答听起来像一只节拍器，倒数着我们被抓或被杀的那天，我想知道我们究竟是真的把旧指挥部抛在了身后，还是只是更长一条可否认链条里的又一支编外部队。我尽量不去想那些我们没问是谁真正签的付款就接下的行动，不去想某些区域在我们自己的地图上总像是被涂黑的。你只能忽视那些图案那么久，之后你就得决定，你是要跟着它们走到尽头，还是用赤手把它们撕开。
